The customerId Stand-In

createTicket needs to know who the customer is — and there's no logged-in user yet to ask.

schema.prisma's Ticket.customerId (one-to-many relations topic) is required, not nullable — every ticket belongs to a customer, by design. But this project has no authentication yet; that's Week 4. Until then, createTicket takes customerId as a perfectly ordinary field in the request body, alongside subject and description:

// Figure 2.15: a temporary stand-in (src/controllers/ticket.controller.js, excerpt)
export const createTicket = asyncHandler(async (req, res) => {
  const { subject, description, customerId } = req.body;

  if (!subject || !description || !customerId) {
    return res
      .status(400)
      .json({ error: { message: 'subject, description and customerId are required' } });
  }

  const ticket = await ticketService.createTicket({
    subject,
    description,
    customerId: Number(customerId),
  });
  res.status(201).json(ticket);
});

This is deliberately a placeholder, not a real design decision — anyone could currently create a ticket "as" any customer id they like, simply by naming a different one in the request body, which is obviously not acceptable for a real API. It's called out here so you're not left wondering whether it was missed: Week 4 replaces this field entirely with req.user.id, read off the authenticated request instead of trusted from the body — the same manual-check style already used for subject and description in Lesson 1, just extended by one more required field for now. Number(customerId) is the same string-to-number conversion req.params.id already needed in the previous lesson — JSON bodies preserve number types, but it costs nothing to be defensive here too.
